content_list.content_text: After the collapse of the Eastern Bloc, Europe entered the 1990s fueled by, among other things, a spirit of artistic freedom. But the economic cost of change was reflected in budget constraints on film production in some countries, limiting costly period dramas to those countries that already had a long track record in the genre.

information.contentText: In 1996, Roberto Benigni, writer-director of Life Is Beautiful, a rival to Train of Life, had been sent the script and offered the role of Shlomo, the "village idiot," by writer-director Mihăileanu, but Benigni turned it down and went on to write and direct Life Is Beautiful. Mihăileanu refuses to discuss publicly whether Benigni plagiarized his film, preferring to say that he and Benigni made "two very different films."

content_list.content_text: The decade began with Jean-Paul Rappeneau's (b. 1932) dazzling adaptation of Cyrano de Bergerac (1990). In a role he and his big nose were born to play, Gérard Depardieu (b. 1948) gave one of his most endearing performances, conveying cunning, intelligence and emotion through Jean-Claude Carrière's dense screenplay.

quote.quote: Gwyneth Paltrow, in her first leading role, creates a heroine so dazzling that she seems entirely plausible as the playwright's guiding light.
quote.author: Janet Maslin on Shakespeare in Love

content_list.content_text: Rappeneau and Carrière teamed up again for Le Hussard sur le toit (The Horseman on the Roof, 1995), billed as the most expensive French film of all time, but lacking the depth of their earlier collaboration. La Reine Margot (Queen Margot, 1994) fared better. Decadent and gory, it felt more like a gangster film than a period drama.

information.contentText: Benigni's friends and those close to him advised him against making the film, since he is a comedian and not Jewish, and since the Holocaust was of no interest to the established audience. Being a gentile, Benigni consulted the Center for Contemporary Jewish Documentation, based in Milan, throughout production. Benigni incorporated historical inaccuracies to distinguish his story from the real Holocaust, about which he said only documentaries showing survivors could provide "the truth."

content_list.content_text: Ismail Merchant (1936-2005) and James Ivory (b. 1928) continued to dominate classic British cinema with two of their finest productions, Howards End (1992) and The Remains of the Day (1993), while Nicholas Hytner (b. 1956) oversaw the successful screen adaptation of Alan Bennett's play in The Madness of King George (1994).

content_list.title: A Fable of Love and Survival
content_list.description:
"Buongiorno Principessa!" Rarely has an expression taken from an Italian film become so well known in every corner of the world. And when it is spoken with arms flung wide by a child leaping out of a cupboard with the burst of joy we see in Guido and Dora's son... it melts anyone's heart. The film from which we borrowed the memory of this scene, as everyone knows, is Life Is Beautiful (1997), and it put actor, director and screenwriter Roberto Benigni in the international spotlight.

The attention Life Is Beautiful drew is explained not only by the many awards it won in Europe and, above all, in Hollywood, but also by the debate it reignited (after Schindler's List (1993)) about the possibilities and limits of representing the Holocaust. The main reason for any controversy was precisely what defines this filmmaker's work: comedy. The Holocaust, it was argued, could not be viewed that way. Benigni reacted to this without bitterness, as can be seen in his answer in a 1999 interview with The Guardian: "We clowns need to be mistreated. It keeps us alive, real. Only a genius like Fellini knew how to do that. He saw clowns as benefactors, saints, as the epitome of tragedy." This same personality that shrugged off bad reviews is the personality of Guido, the protagonist of Life Is Beautiful, played by Benigni, who bursts into the film with infectious enthusiasm. We know it won't all be roses, because the opening line serves as a warning: "This is a simple story, but not an easy one to tell. Like a fable, there is sorrow, and like a fable, it is full of wonder and happiness."

Roberto Benigni's reasons for making this film were neither political nor historical, although he and screenwriter Vincenzo Cerami (b. 1940) took the precaution of hiring consultants from the Center for Jewish Documentation in Milan and holding screenings for groups of Italian Jews before the release. His desire to tell a story of love and humanity in an extreme context needed only this, so to speak, scientific confirmation to launch into international distribution. And its success was confirmed in Cannes, Warsaw, the United States and even Jerusalem, where the film later won the "Best Jewish Experience" award at the Jerusalem Film Festival. The great human inspiration behind Life Is Beautiful was Rubino Romeo Salmonì (1920-2011). It was the story of this Italian Jew, captured by the Nazis in 1943, that caught Benigni's attention through the book Ho sconfitto Hitler (literally, I Defeated Hitler), in which he recounts how he survived Auschwitz. Before putting it into writing, Rubino shared his experience with children and teenagers, doing so in a more optimistic way, as the book reveals, adopting a tone of a certain irony. And it was this man's strong, confident spirit (one that never forgot comedy) that suggested the possibility of talking about love in the most catastrophic of situations. It is no accident that the film's seemingly trivial title also has a very specific origin: it was taken from the sentence with which Leon Trotsky ended his testament, written in Mexico: "Life is beautiful. Let the future generations cleanse it of all evil, oppression and violence, and enjoy it to the full."

Moreover, inventiveness in the service of humanism, far more than historical accuracy, was the main symbol of the campaign to spread the film around the world, and especially in the United States, where the term "Italian fable" circulated with the director's full approval; he only added that "it was invented from the truth." By the time it reached the Oscars in 1999, Life Is Beautiful was already the highest-grossing foreign-language film of all time in the North American market: 21 million dollars.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the article "A Vida é Bela: uma fábula de amor e sobrevivência" (Life Is Beautiful: A Fable of Love and Survival), by Inês Lourenço in Diário de Notícias.

content_list.content_text: Kenneth Branagh (b. 1960) followed up his blood-and-mud version of Henry V (1989) with Much Ado About Nothing (1993), the best Shakespeare adaptation of the decade, with the exception of Baz Luhrmann's (b. 1962) brilliant take on Romeo + Juliet (1996). Branagh's Hamlet (1996), however, the first to use Shakespeare's complete text, was only a partial success. Shakespeare in Love (1998), co-written by playwright Tom Stoppard (b. 1937), proved even more popular, captivating audiences and winning the Oscars for Best Picture and Best Original Screenplay. Derek Jarman (1942-1994) produced one of his finest works in 1991, an adaptation of another Elizabethan drama, Christopher Marlowe's Edward II.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from Much Ado About Nothing
information.contentText: Despite its faithfulness, a few things were overlooked: an accordion appears at the masked ball, although this instrument was not invented until 1822; except for those in the foreground in one shot sequence, the lanterns at the masked ball are lit by electric bulbs; and the deck chair was first patented in the late 19th century, so it would not have been available at the time the film is set.

content_list.content_text: Many European countries examined more recent events. Michael Collins (1996) and Some Mother's Son (1996) turned their gaze to aspects of the Irish Troubles. Germany's small output of period films in the 1990s, which included Aimée & Jaguar (1999) and the delicate Europa Europa (1990), the latter directed by Agnieszka Holland (b. 1948), drew on events of World War II.

quote.quote: Ultimately, no matter how many innovative and unconventional flourishes he applies, the success of any adaptation of a Shakespeare play is determined by two factors: the competence of the director and the ability of the principal cast members. Luhrmann, Danes, and DiCaprio put this Romeo + Juliet in good hands.
quote.author: James Berardinelli on Romeo + Juliet

content_list.content_text: The most important Spanish period film of the decade was the Oscar-winning Belle époque (1992). La lengua de las mariposas (Butterfly, 1999) and Ken Loach's (b. 1936) Land and Freedom (1995) focused on the Spanish Civil War, while Vacas (Cows, 1992) told the eccentric story of a Basque family over seven decades. A similar narrative structure was adopted by Hungarian director István Szabó (b. 1938) in Sunshine (1999), and with even better results by the Greek Theo Angelopoulos (b. 1935) in To Vlemma tou Odyssea (Ulysses' Gaze, 1995).

information.contentText: Luhrmann secured some funding from Fox to hold a workshop and shoot some teaser footage in Sydney. Leonardo DiCaprio agreed to pay his own expenses to fly to Sydney and take part. Once Fox saw the fight scene, they agreed to back the film.

content_list.content_text: Il postino (The Postman, 1994), a fictional account of the meeting between Pablo Neruda and a lovestruck postman, was one of the most internationally successful Italian productions, though it was soon overshadowed by La vita è bella (Life Is Beautiful, 1997), directed by and starring Roberto Benigni (b. 1952). The comedy-drama, set mostly in a concentration camp, was one of the decade's biggest period-film hits, although opinions on its merits remain divided.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Ian Haydn Smith, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

movies.title: Life Is Beautiful
movies.overview: A touching story of an Italian book seller of Jewish ancestry who lives in his own little fairy tale. His creative and happy life would come to an abrupt halt when his entire family is deported to a concentration camp during World War II. While locked up he tries to convince his son that the whole thing is just a game.

movies.title: Shakespeare in Love
movies.overview: Young Shakespeare is forced to stage his latest comedy, "Romeo and Ethel, the Pirate's Daughter," before it's even written. When a lovely noblewoman auditions for a role, they fall into forbidden love -- and his play finds a new life (and title). As their relationship progresses, Shakespeare's comedy soon transforms into tragedy.

movies.title: Romeo + Juliet
movies.overview: In director Baz Luhrmann's contemporary take on William Shakespeare's classic tragedy, the Montagues and Capulets have moved their ongoing feud to the sweltering suburb of Verona Beach, where Romeo and Juliet fall in love and secretly wed. Though the film is visually modern, the bard's dialogue remains.

movies.title: Cyrano de Bergerac
movies.overview: Embarrassed by his large nose, a romantic poet/soldier romances his cousin by proxy.

movies.title: Much Ado About Nothing
movies.overview: In this Shakespearean farce, Hero and her groom-to-be, Claudio, team up with Claudio's commanding officer, Don Pedro, the week before their wedding to hatch a matchmaking scheme. Their targets are sharp-witted duo Benedick and Beatrice -- a tough task indeed, considering their corresponding distaste for love and each other. Meanwhile, meddling Don John plots to ruin the wedding.

movies.title: The Postman
movies.overview: Simple Italian postman learns to love poetry while delivering mail to a famous poet; he uses this to woo local beauty Beatrice.

movies.title: Land and Freedom
movies.overview: David Carr is a British Communist who is unemployed. In 1936, when the Spanish Civil War begins, he decides to fight for the Republican side, a coalition of liberals, communists and anarchists, so he joins the POUM militia and witnesses firsthand the betrayal of the Spanish revolution by Stalin's followers and Moscow's orders.

movies.title: The Horseman on the Roof
movies.overview: In a time of war and disease, a young officer gallantly tries to help a young woman find her husband.

movies.title: Queen Margot
movies.overview: The night of August 24, 1572, is known as the Massacre of St. Bartholomew. In France a religious war is raging. In order to impose peace a forced wedding is arranged between Margot de Valois, sister of the immature Catholic King Charles IX, and the Hugenot King Henri of Navarre. Catherine of Medici maintains her behind-the-scenes power by ordering assaults, poisonings, and instigations to incest.

movies.title: The Madness of King George
movies.overview: King George III's erratic behaviour leads to a plot in Parliament to have him declared insane and removed from the throne.

movies.title: Hamlet
movies.overview: Hamlet, Prince of Denmark, returns home to find his father murdered and his mother now marrying the murderer... his uncle. Meanwhile, war is brewing.

movies.title: Europa Europa
movies.overview: A Jewish boy separated from his family in the early days of WWII poses as a German orphan and is taken into the heart of the Nazi world as a 'war hero' and eventually becomes a Hitler Youth. Although improbabilities and happenstance are cornerstones of the film, it is based upon a true story.

content_list.title: Timeline of Events from 1990 to 2009
content_list.description: '90s independent cinema dominates the screens, and animation breaks new ground with Pixar. CGI reaches a new level with The Matrix, and Latin American and European cinemas capture the world's attention. Click here to see a chronological view of the main events in cinema from 1990 to 2009.
